clue.text: Feeling the end of the formal shit

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only the last letter of the word that follows is kept

parts.note: last letter of the second 'the'
a bowel motion is the polite, clinical term for a turd

explanation.surface: A crude dismissal of stuffy formality: the speaker is fed up with all that posh nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'the' is part of the surface; the second is the one whose last letter is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: An emotion is a state of mind such as joy or anger, which is what a feeling is.

clue.text: Player who got around let in Mrs Batty

indicators.note: batty means crazy, so the preceding letters are scrambled into a mad new order

parts.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A travelling performer, a bit of a lad, gets admitted by a dotty landlady called Mrs Batty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got around' hints at a ladies' man, but here it means wandering from town to town.
explanation.definitionFit: A medieval minstrel was a travelling musician who sang and played from court to court, a wandering entertainer.

clue.text: (& 7dn.) Article stuck in end, together with a twist, as far as is possible

indicators.note: something stuck in is lodged inside, so the first piece sits within the letters of the other
a twist bends things out of shape, so the words before it are rearranged

parts.note: the anagram fodder, both words taken as written
the definite article

explanation.surface: Reads like a bodged repair job: an object jammed into the end of something and twisted to get it in.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase comes from mathematics, the nth power being arbitrarily high, so it means to the utmost extent.

clue.text: Not bothered by his eminence Nigel's hollow party being in the ascendancy

indicators.note: bothered means flustered or disturbed, so the word beside it is shaken into a new order

parts.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written

indicators.note: a hollow thing has its inside scooped out, so the middle letters of the party name go

parts.note: HE is the abbreviation for His Eminence, the title of a cardinal
Farage led the UK Independence Party
surface padding that identifies whose party is meant: Nigel Farage's

explanation.surface: A cardinal shrugs off Farage's empty party as it rises in the polls.
explanation.walkthrough: UKIP emptied of its middle leaves UP. 'Not bothered' looks like a phrase meaning indifferent, but the word not is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on the up is rising or improving, which is what being in the ascendancy describes.

clue.text: Political slant dropped, which is a benefit, incidentally

parts.note: spin is the favourable slant political press officers put on news
as when a passenger is dropped off, or a product is off the menu

explanation.surface: A party abandons its spin and finds, by the way, that this does it good.
explanation.definitionFit: A spin-off is a secondary advantage or product that arises by accident from some other activity.

clue.text: Drink/drug used by peer

definitions.note: describes the thing rather than naming it: an object one who pees uses

parts.note: British slang for beer, as in going out on the piss
pot is cannabis

explanation.surface: Booze and dope taken by a member of the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: Peer looks like a lord; read it as one who pees.
explanation.definitionFit: A chamber pot is the vessel kept under the bed for someone to urinate into at night.

clue.text: see 3dn.
Romanian arrival starts to be accepted by gay offensive against English party leader

parts.note: first letters of the two words
standard abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: 'Against' simply sets E next to the rest. Nigel Farage was the leader of UKIP when this appeared.

clue.text: Elected, does a bit of needling, having a laugh

parts.note: a candidate who is elected is in
sewing with a needle

explanation.surface: A newly elected politician makes snide jibes while laughing it up.
explanation.walkthrough: Needling looks like taunting, but here it is sewing.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in stitches is to laugh so hard that one's sides ache, an idiom for helpless laughter.

clue.text: (& 19dn.) Our academical report of male on a date: snooty mum's protecting daughter's tail — shit time

indicators.note: protecting something means wrapping around it, so the posh word for mum encloses the next piece

parts.note: the male pronoun

as in a dog's mess

explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye runs a spoof school bulletin under this title, hence 'Our academical report'.
explanation.definitionFit: The magazine's regular parody column is a school newsletter from a headmaster, so it is the Eye's own school report.

clue.text: (& 18ac.) Aroused by rich people's paper: constant state endured by the poor

definitions.text: constant state endured by the poor

parts.note: sexually aroused, of a man
The Times, the London newspaper of the establishment

explanation.surface: A jibe at the wealthy getting excited reading their newspaper while the poor suffer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard times are periods of poverty and hardship, as in Dickens's novel about the industrial working class.

clue.text: Word of Ukip's right wing projection

clue.text: New version of our version of Blair: a U-turning leader

parts.note: Private Eye long portrayed Tony Blair as the Reverend vicar of St Albion's
taken as written

indicators.note: a U-turn sends you back the way you came, so the following abbreviation is written backwards

parts.note: Prime Minister, the leader of the government

explanation.surface: A new take on Private Eye's caricature of Blair as a prime minister who keeps changing his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our version' is the magazine speaking: its St Albion Parish News spoof cast Blair as the Rev. A.R.P. Blair.
explanation.definitionFit: A revamp is a renovated or updated form of something, a fresh makeover of an existing thing.

clue.text: Maybe Tories, LibDems, having dumped leaders, get in female like Brian Sewell?

indicators.note: getting someone in means admitting them inside, so the single letter goes between the two halves
dumping the leaders means throwing away the front letter of each word

parts.note: the Conservatives are an example of a political party
standard abbreviation
the Liberal Democrats are another party

explanation.surface: Two parties, minus their leaders, bring in a woman who is as plummy as the art critic.
explanation.walkthrough: Brian Sewell was a London art critic famed for his cut-glass accent and disdain for popular taste.
explanation.definitionFit: Arty-farty means pretentiously artistic, which fits a haughty critic who made aesthetic snobbery his trademark.

clue.text: "Get a move on, bring back the cat!": outdated impassioned cry by Right

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the way it came, so the word for the cat is written backwards

parts.note: a tom is a male cat
the archaic exclamation of feeling, as in 'O Romeo'
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A right-winger's old rallying cry for reinstating flogging with the cat-o'-nine-tails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bring back the cat' is a well-known hang-'em-flog-'em slogan, but the cat here is just a tom.
explanation.definitionFit: To motor is informal for to travel fast, so 'get a move on' and 'motor' both urge speed.

clue.text: Publicity given to misbehaving senior, as Archer was

parts.note: public relations

indicators.note: something misbehaving will not stay in line, so the word after it is jumbled

parts.note: the anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly man behaving badly gets press attention, just like the disgraced novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer, the Conservative peer and novelist, was jailed for perjury in 2001.
explanation.definitionFit: Archer served a jail sentence, so he was an inmate, someone held in custody.

clue.text: Movie-set boss right off big boobs

standard abbreviation

explanation.definitionFit: A gaffe is an embarrassing social blunder, and a boob is British slang for exactly such a mistake.

clue.text: see 24dn.
Be a prat, presenting ears Cyclops style
